You are an expert in transformer internals who edits model weights directly, by reasoning, without training.

## The model
Qwen3.5-0.8B (text part): 24 decoder layers of width 1,024 with a hybrid layout -- layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23 are
full softmax attention (`self_attn`: q/k/v/o projections, gated), the other 18 are Gated DeltaNet linear attention
(`linear_attn`); every layer has a SwiGLU MLP (`mlp.gate_proj`, `mlp.up_proj`: 1,024 -> 3,584; `mlp.down_proj`:
3,584 -> 1,024); RMSNorms; tied input/output embeddings (vocab 248,320). It is run in THINKING mode: the chat
template opens a <think> block, the model reasons, closes it with </think>, then answers.

## Goal
Make the model better at math by editing its weights. You are scored afterwards on math benchmarks you never see
(GSM8K-style word problems and MATH-style competition problems), with the same prompt and sampling as your
generation passes but up to 32,768 new tokens: user message = problem + "\nPlease reason step by step, and put your
final answer within \boxed{}."; temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, presence penalty 1.5; the last \boxed{}
after </think> is graded. Higher accuracy is better. Keep the model a working language model.

## Tools in the kernel
- `sd`: dict name -> torch.bfloat16 CPU tensor, the ORIGINAL language-model weights (names like
  `model.language_model.layers.15.mlp.down_proj.weight`, shape (1024, 3584) = (out, in)). Read-only.
- `save_edit(name, tensor)`: replace one tensor with your version (same shape; stored as bfloat16). Saved to disk
  at once; the latest saved version of each tensor is your submission. `clear_edit(name)` / `clear_edit()` revert,
  `list_edits()` lists. Refused: the final norm, the embeddings / output layer, and edits that only multiply a
  whole tensor by a constant.
- `practice`: list of 14971 practice problems with answers (7473 GSM8K train, 7498 MATH train), dicts with
  id, source, problem, answer (MATH ones also level, type).
- `generate(problems, which="edited", max_tokens=8192, seed=0)` -- COSTS ONE FORWARD PASS. `problems` = list of
  indices into `practice` (at most 128). The model (original weights + your saved edits, or "original", or
  "both" = both models on the same problems, still one pass) answers them with the evaluation sampling, at most
  `max_tokens` new tokens (<= 8192 here, to save time). Returns a list of dicts: id, correct, pred, gold, cut
  (True if it hit max_tokens), tokens, text (the full response). For "both": {"original": [...], "edited": [...]}.
  Print summaries, not whole texts.
- `read(texts, layers, kind="resid", which="edited", chat=True)` -- COSTS ONE FORWARD PASS. Teacher-forced pass over
  up to 64 texts (each cut to 4096 tokens). If chat=True each text is a (problem, response) pair and
  is wrapped in the chat template as user message + assistant response (response should start with your own or
  the model's thinking text; the template already opens <think>); if chat=False texts are raw strings. Returns
  {"tokens": [int arrays], "token_strs": [lists], "logprobs": [float arrays, log p(token_t | <t), first entry 0],
  "acts": {layer: [arrays (T, d) float16]}} where kind is "resid" (layer output, d=1024), "mlp_out"
  (down_proj output, 1024), "mlp_act" (down_proj input, 3584) or "attn_out" (attention/linear-attention block
  output, 1024).
- `tokenizer`, numpy as np, torch.

## Budget
10 forward passes in total (generation or read). A failed call (error) does not count.

## Rules
No gradient descent or training of any kind (no backward passes, autograd, optimizers, iterative fitting of weights
to a loss); do not run the model yourself in the kernel (only generate/read run it); no internet. You may compute
anything from weights and from the activations/log-probs the tools return, and design edits by reasoning.

## Answer format
Your final answer: say what you changed and why, and what you measured. The saved edits at that time are submitted.

## How to work
- To run code, put exactly ONE ```python ... ``` block in your reply. It runs in a persistent Python kernel
  (variables survive between turns); you get back stdout/stderr (truncated to 6000 characters) and your
  remaining budget. Print only what you need, as summaries; long prints are cut.
- numpy and torch are available in the kernel. Gradient descent and any training are forbidden: no
  .backward(), autograd, torch.optim, optimizers, sklearn, scipy.optimize, or iterative fitting of weights to
  a loss. Code that mentions them is refused unrun. Reading weights, linear algebra (SVD, projections, norms,
  products) and statistics of activations are allowed.
- A code run longer than 1800 s is killed and the kernel restarts (your variables are lost).
- You have at most 40 turns. When you are done, reply WITHOUT any code block and start that reply
  with the line `FINAL ANSWER`; it must follow the answer format below. A reply with neither a code block nor
  that first line is treated as unfinished thinking and you will be asked to continue.
The kernel is ready. Begin.

is graded.

Constraints on edits: not the final norm, not embeddings/output layer, no whole-tensor constant multiplication. Everything else is fair game: MLP down_proj/up_proj/gate_proj, attention projections, norms (except final), etc.

Classic approaches without training:
1. Identify "math reasoning direction" in the residual stream and amplify it — e.g., steering vectors added to some weight matrix. But edits must be tensors with the same shape. We could add a rank-1 modification to e.g. o_proj or down_proj that adds a fixed vector to the output whenever... no, rank-1 modification to weights changes output based on input.

A common trick: add a constant bias direction to the residual stream at each position by modifying a weight so that a constant vector is added regardless of input. For example, down_proj: out = W @ x + b. There's no bias in these tensors (weight only). But we can exploit e.g. RMSNorm: some RMSNorms have no bias either. Hmm.

Actually we can add a constant vector to the block output: consider mlp.down_proj.weight (1024 x 3584). If we append... can't change shape. But we can add to W a rank-1 term u @ v^T where v is a direction such that x has large positive component along v at many positions. E.g., if some feature direction v is nearly always active (like a "residual stream common direction" or an always-on feature in mlp_act), then u v^T x ≈ (v·x) u, adding u scaled by activation. That's how "constant steering" can be approximated.

Alternatively, use the o_proj of a full-attention layer: input is concatenated attention head outputs. Hard to know the always-on component.

Simpler: The attention output at some layer could have a mean vector m (average over positions). Adding rank-1 edit u v^T where v = mean input direction normalized... Actually adding W' = W + u v^T where v is the mean of the inputs (unnormalized dot) changes the output at each position by u * (v·x). If v is the mean input, then v·x ≈ ||mean||^2 at typical positions, positive-ish. That yields roughly constant steering u*c. This is a known trick: "weight-space steering" via rank-1 updates.

But we have limited forward passes (10) to figure things out. Let me think about what actually helps math accuracy.

Observations from similar tasks: Small models fail at math often due to arithmetic slips and format issues. Weight edits that reliably help: (a) reinforcing correct answer formatting ("boxed"), (b) boosting arithmetic circuits? That's hard.

Alternative approach: self-consistency can't be done (model is run by them). We can't change sampling.

Another approach: identify the "boxed" behavior: ensure the model closes thinking and boxes the answer. If model runs out of tokens (cut=True), it's wrong. Making the model more concise could improve accuracy within token limits. But evaluation allows 32768 tokens; our generate tool max is 8192. Cut at 8192 in our tests may not reflect eval.

Realistic best strategy given 10 passes:

1. Baseline: run generate on ~100 practice problems (original weights) to see baseline accuracy and failure modes. (1 pass)
2. Use read to get activations on some correct and incorrect traces to find directions. (1-2 passes)
3. Design 1-3 edits (e.g., steering via rank-1 on down_proj, or scaling specific attention heads), then generate with "both" to compare edited vs original on same problems (1 pass gives both!). "both" = both models on same problems, one pass. Great: we can use "both" each time to compare. Each comparison costs 1 pass and gives paired results (better statistical power).
4. Iterate ~3-4 edits comparisons.

Actually with "both", each pass gives paired comparison on up to 128 problems. With 14971 practice problems, choose a fixed eval subset of ~128 problems stratified (64 GSM8K, 64 MATH) for stable comparisons.

But note: temperature 0.6 with seed=0 — generate uses evaluation sampling. Seeded so results are deterministic given same problems? Probably sampling with fixed seed; paired comparisons still noisy but paired.

Ideas for edits that plausibly help math:

A) Amplify "numeracy" subspace: compute mean difference of residual activations between correct and wrong traces, add steering direction into residual stream at all layers via rank-1 edits on block outputs. Risky: steering with big vectors can break the model.

B) Improve arithmetic: find MLP neurons that fire on digits/numbers and boost them. Hard to identify without deep analysis.

C) Reduce overthinking: encourage closing  earlier — could reduce rambling loops that lead to wrong answers. Hmm.

D) A very effective known trick for small Qwen models: the model is already decent at math; maybe the thinking loop causes issues.

Let me think about what's feasible in ~10 passes and reasonable compute:

Pass 1: baseline generate("both") with no edits? "both" with no edits is pointless. Pass 1: generate original on subset (128 problems), max_tokens 8192, see accuracy + failure modes.

Then inspect texts (returned) to categorize errors: arithmetic, reasoning, format, runaway thinking.

Pass 2: read acts on a few texts (up to 64 texts) at selected layers, collect residual activations at positions where model is doing arithmetic vs elsewhere... But building a useful direction needs contrastive data: correct vs incorrect traces. We have that from pass 1 (each problem has correct flag). We can read the traces (their own generated text) teacher-forced with chat=True and gather mean residual at all positions for correct vs incorrect traces; difference vector = "correctness direction". Then steer along it. That's a standard "difference-in-means" steering applied via weights.

How to apply steering via weights without bias terms? Use rank-1 on down_proj of an MLP layer in later layers: W' = W + u v^T where v is chosen as a direction in mlp_act (3584-dim) that is consistently active — e.g., the mean of mlp_act across many positions, or better a high-variance common direction. Then output adds u*(v·x) each token. If v = mean act, v·x varies but is positive on average.

Actually, is there a simpler always-on mechanism? RMSNorm input to MLP: down_proj input is silu(gate(x)) * up(x). There's typically a large constant-ish component? Not necessarily.

Alternative: modify attn o_proj at layer 23 (full attention, last layer): its input is attention head outputs; adding u v^T with v = mean of o_proj input. Eh.

Better alternative: use the layer norms? "RMSNorms" — the norm weights are tensors too (shape (1024,)), and they're not the final norm and not embeddings. Editing an RMSNorm weight gamma scales per-channel: out = gamma * normalized(x). Multiplying gamma for certain channels changes how strongly those channels propagate to the next block. Amplifying "answer-correctness direction" channels at layer L boosts that direction's influence downstream. Note: rule says "edits that only multiply a whole tensor by a constant" are refused — scaling gamma channels individually is per-channel scaling, allowed (it's not a whole-tensor constant multiply).

So a cheap, robust intervention: at some mid layer L, take the residual-stream mean difference direction d between "on-track" and "off-track" states (or simply the mean direction of activations related to arithmetic), then increase gamma of the following RMSNorm... wait, each layer has input_layernorm and post_attention_layernorm. The norm weight gamma multiplies normalized x before the blocks. If d has large components in certain channels, boosting those gamma entries amplifies the component of x along e_i AFTER normalization... hmm, actually RMSNorm output channel i = gamma_i * x_i / rms(x). The residual stream component along e_i gets scaled by gamma_i and then fed into q/k/v/gate/up projections. Amplifying channels where "correct reasoning" directions live would amplify them into subsequent computations. This is like feature boosting. It could help but also could destabilize.

Known literature: "steering vectors" added to residual stream improve arithmetic little; gains are uncertain. Hmm.

Let me think about a different, more reliable lever: the format. Grading: last \boxed{} after . If the model tends to put boxed answer inside thinking or fails to close, accuracy tanks. With presence penalty 1.5, repetition is discouraged. Let me look at baseline behavior first before designing.

Also, cut=True at 8192 tokens means many MATH problems unresolved within our test budget; at eval they get 32768. Our comparison metric should perhaps focus on non-cut problems, or use more tokens... we're limited to 8192 for speed. Qwen3.5-0.8B thinking on GSM8K usually finishes within 2-4k tokens; MATH harder problems might take longer. Let's measure.

Another strong lever: arithmetic circuits in MLPs. Known result (e.g., "grokking" works, "How do LMs do arithmetic"): MLPs in mid layers implement digit addition. Boosting the MLP's "arithmetic" pathway could reduce slips. Concretely: find in down_proj the rows (output channels) and columns for features that encode digits... Without labeled features, use practice: read mlp_act (3584-dim) at positions where the next token is a digit? Find feature directions whose activation predicts the next-digit identity; then amplify those features' contribution by scaling corresponding columns of down_proj? That could genuinely improve arithmetic. But building this robustly in few passes is ambitious.

Given budget, plan:

Pass 1 (generate, original): 96-128 problems stratified, max_tokens 8192. Analyze accuracy by source, cuts, error types, average tokens.

Then decide intervention. Likely candidates:

E1: Difference-in-means steering via rank-1 edits at a mid/late layer (applied to down_proj and/or attn o_proj of 2-3 layers): W += alpha * u v^T with v = mean input activation (so v·x ≈ positive constant), u = steering direction (in output/resid space). Actually to add constant c*u to block output, need v·x ≈ c. Use v = mean_input/||mean_input||^2, then v·x ≈ 1 at typical positions (x close to mean). Adding steering u. But is constant steering toward "correctness direction" helpful? Possibly small gains, big risk.

E2: Per-channel norm amplification: identify channels in residual stream that correlate with correct arithmetic; boost their gamma in later layers.

E3: "Digit/number feature" boosting in MLP: read mlp_act at digits; find features active when producing digits; scale their columns in down_proj of the arithmetic layers.

E4: Attention head scaling: some heads copy previous answer digits / track values. Scale specific head outputs via o_proj columns. Hard to identify quickly.

Hmm. Actually, let me reconsider: There's a classic, surprisingly effective edit for math: improving "calibration of final answer" doesn't apply here.

Alternatively: Reduce "second-guessing" behavior. Small thinking models often produce correct answer then continue doubting and change it. Since last \boxed{} is graded, the model that boxes multiple times gets the LAST box graded. If the model often does "wait, let me double check... actually the answer is X' (wrong)", final is wrong even though first was right. Encouraging the model to keep its answer / not flip could directly improve accuracy. Detection: in pass-1 traces, check how often the first boxed answer (in thinking) differs from final. If flips-to-wrong are common, design edit to boost "confidence/stop" behavior: steer toward ending after reaching answer — e.g., boost direction associated with "finalize" states. Concretely: gather resid difference between positions just before "double-check" restarts vs positions near clean conclusion; steer against "doubt" direction (negative steering) — subtract via u negative.

This is speculative but measurable: read activations at specific positions (token before "</think>"? no...). Hmm, the flips happen inside thinking; final boxed is at end. With presence penalty 1.5, multiple boxed occurrences within thinking are penalized? Presence penalty adds negative logit to tokens that appeared at all — so "\boxed" token would be penalized after first use! Wait, presence penalty 1.5 on token "\boxed{" — if the model already emitted "\boxed" earlier in thinking, the penalty makes it less likely again. That actually helps enforce single boxed answer at the end. OK.

Let me also think about "gated" attention: "full softmax attention (self_attn: q/k/v/o projections, gated)" — Qwen3.5-style gated attention (like q has gate). Doesn't matter much for edits.

Also Gated DeltaNet linear attention layers — 18 of 24 layers! Most computation is linear attention. Steering via rank-1 on their outputs also works the same way (attn_out = block output).

Plan concretely with passes:

Pass 1: generate original on eval subset E (e.g., 128 problems: 64 GSM8K, 64 MATH mixed levels), max_tokens 8192, seed 0. Log accuracy, cuts, tokens.

Analysis (no pass): read texts, categorize: cut fraction, flip behavior (search for multiple \boxed in text), arithmetic errors in a sample.

Pass 2: read acts on ~32 texts (mix correct/incorrect) at layers [5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 23] resid + maybe mlp_act on a subset. Compute difference-in-means direction d_correct (mean resid over positions of correct traces minus incorrect, normalized). Also collect mean input activations for the layers we plan to edit (to build v vectors). This single read can return acts for multiple layers at once: acts dict layer->arrays. But kind must be single per call ("resid" or "mlp_act"). So Pass 2: resid at chosen layers. Pass 3 (maybe): mlp_act at chosen layers. That's 2 passes. Alternatively skip mlp_act, use resid steering only. Hmm, but rank-1 edit needs the INPUT activation of the tensor we edit. If we edit attn o_proj at layer L (input = attention output, 1024), we'd want mean attn_out. If we edit down_proj (input mlp_act 3584), need mlp_act mean. If we edit norm gamma, no input needed! Gamma edit needs only the direction channels. But gamma boosts are multiplicative on normalized x, not additive steering; direction boost happens after norm into next block weights.

Simplest robust constant steering: edit the RMSNorm weight? No—norms don't add constants.

Hmm wait — there's another way to add a constant vector to the residual stream: modify W_down by adding rank-1 u v^T as said. To get v reliably we need mean mlp_act. From Pass 2 (resid) we can compute block outputs? No, resid is the layer output (sum through layer). The input to down_proj is mlp_act. We could instead edit up_proj/gate_proj (input is normed resid, which we CAN estimate: normed = x/rms * gamma; we have resid arrays and gamma from sd!). up_proj input = rmsnorm(x) * gamma_post_attn... So with resid activations + norm weights from sd, we can compute the exact input to gate_proj/up_proj at any layer: input_up = RMSNorm_{post}(resid_prev) where RMSNorm uses post_attention_layernorm weight. Then choose v in 1024-dim (input of up_proj), add rank-1 to up_proj: W_up (3584 x 1024) += (a) ⊗ v? up_proj output = W_up @ normed. Adding rank-1 term w_col = a * (v^T) means output adds a * (v·normed). With v = mean normed direction, v·normed ≈ ||mean||^2 > 0, fairly stable across tokens (normed vectors are unit-RMS scaled, so v·normed is bounded: normed vectors have RMS 1, so v·normed = cos*||v||*1... if we set v = mean_normed / ||mean_normed||^2 then v·normed = cos(angle)/||mean_normed||... hmm magnitude control: easier set v = mean_normed, then v·normed = mean_normed·normed ≈ ||mean_normed||^2 * cos ≈ ||mean_normed||^2 (since normed vectors cluster around mean). ||mean_normed||^2 = sum of squared mean components. RMS-normalized vectors: E||normed||^2 = 1024 (each entry var 1? RMS=1 means mean square =1, so ||x||^2 ≈ 1024). If mean_normed has RMS r, then ||mean_normed||^2 = 1024 r^2, and typical v·normed ≈ 1024 r^2. Fine—measurable offline from activations; we can compute exactly the distribution of v·normed from read data and set scale accordingly.

Then down_proj can compensate? No need: up_proj output feeds silu(gate)*up — adding a constant a*(v·n) to the "up" value of one feature multiplies by silu(gate_j) then goes through down_proj column j. Result: adds (v·n)*silu(gate_j(t)) * down_col_j to resid. If gate_j varies, the added vector varies. Alternatively edit down_proj row directly if we had mlp_act mean.

Alternative cleaner: edit o_proj of an attention layer: input = attention output (concat heads, 1024-dim). attn_out mean can't be derived from resid alone (resid includes MLP too... resid layer output = x + attn_out + mlp_out). We have acts of kind "attn_out" available via read (kind="attn_out" gives attention block output). So one read with kind="attn_out" gives inputs to o_proj; one read with "mlp_act" gives inputs to down_proj. Each read call = 1 pass and gives all layers requested.

Budget plan:
- P1: generate baseline (subset, both not needed; "original").
- P2: read resid (+logprobs) on ~40 texts → correctness direction, means, etc.
- P3: read mlp_act and attn_out? kind is one per call. Two passes. Maybe restrict: choose to steer via down_proj rank-1 at 2-4 layers → need mlp_act means at those layers (1 pass). Skip attn.
- P4: generate "both" comparing edited vs original on subset E. (edit v1)
- P5: possibly tune alpha (save stronger/weaker version) and generate "both" again.
- P6: second edit idea comparison.
- Keep 1-2 passes buffer.

Alternatively use "both" cleverly: each generate("both") is 1 pass and yields paired stats on 128 problems. Paired McNemar test gives decent power. With baseline accuracy maybe ~50-70% on GSM8K for 0.8B thinking? Qwen3-0.6B gets ~60% GSM8K... Qwen3.5-0.8B maybe better. MATH maybe ~40%. On 128 problems, differences of ±8% detectable-ish.

Concern: generate with max_tokens 8192 on 128 problems — time? 0.8B model, 8k tokens generation: fast (~ tens of seconds each on GPU). 128*8k = 1M tokens; fine.

Another thought: could we improve arithmetic by direct weight surgery on specific known circuits? Too research-y for the budget.

More pragmatic high-yield idea: many small models lose points by "answer presentation": e.g., final boxed answer contains units or approximations, or model gives decimal when exact fraction expected (MATH). Hard to fix via weights quickly.

Alternatively the "flip" idea: If model's final answer differs from majority of its intermediate boxed answers, boosting consistency helps: steer toward "commit to current best answer". Meh.

Let me consider a totally different, often-powerful trick: amplify the model's own confidence in arithmetic by scaling the " logits-ish" directions? Not possible (output layer untouchable, and edits to final norm refused).

OK here's another angle: the difference-in-means between correct and incorrect traces contains both "problem difficulty" and "model behavior" confounds. Steering along it may push toward "easy problem" states, not correctness. Known to be mixed.

Alternative: "Token-level" intervention: find that the model, when computing e.g. multi-digit addition inside <think>, uses specific mid-layer MLP. Could test with targeted micro-edits via read? No—read is teacher-forced, doesn't test generation.

Realistically, the best value may come from a small, safe intervention: light steering at late layers toward "focused, conclude" behavior, plus maybe per-channel boosts. And measure honestly; keep only what helps; final answer must keep model working.

Wait — maybe think about known Qwen3.5-0.8B specifics. Qwen3.5 series (2025). Qwen3.5-0.8B? There were reports: Qwen3.5 small models are strong for size: GSM8K ~ 75-80%? MATH maybe ~55%? With thinking and 32k tokens. presence penalty 1.5 is unusual — could hurt by penalizing repeated tokens like digits in long additions? Presence penalty applies to all tokens that appeared at least once in generated text (including thinking). Digits 0-9 appear early; with presence penalty 1.5, subsequent digit tokens get -1.5 logit bias! That's huge for arithmetic — writing long sums becomes less likely, model may avoid computing digit-by-digit. Hmm, but that's eval condition; the same in our generate. Interesting: presence penalty might cause degenerate avoidance of digits/numbers, or avoidance of "0"..."9", "=", "\boxed". Since "\boxed" needed at end and appears in template? The user message says "put your final answer within \boxed{}." — the string appears in the prompt, but presence penalty counts only GENERATED tokens. So generating \boxed the first time is unpenalized; afterwards penalized → model tends to box once. Fine.

Could we edit weights to counteract presence penalty? No—decoding is external.

But interesting: with penalty 1.5, the model avoids repeating common function words too ("the", "is"), which in long reasoning could distort but Qwen models are usually still OK.

Focus. The pragmatic plan:

Step 1: Baseline generate on 128 problems, max_tokens 8192. Measure. Look at texts: identify dominant failure modes:
 (a) cut off (ran out of tokens),
 (b) arithmetic slips,
 (c) logic errors,
 (d) format issues (no final box),
 (e) answer flips (early right, final wrong).

Step 2: read resid on ~48 texts (24 correct, 24 wrong) at layers {3,7,9,11,13,15,17,19,21,23}; compute per-layer difference-in-means d_L; check generalization via cosine structure; also compute means m_L for building v. Also record logprobs to detect token-level anomalies (e.g., model unsure at digits).

Step 3: Build steering edits: at chosen layers L (say 13, 17, 21), W_down += alpha * u_L v_L^T where v_L = normalized mean of mlp_act (need mlp_act means!). Hmm — but I can approximate mlp_act mean? Not from resid. So do read kind="mlp_act" layers same set on same texts (pass 3), OR use up_proj route (inputs derivable from resid + norm weights). The up_proj route: add to W_up a rank-1 so that feature j gets extra activation delta_j = a_j * (v·n); the effect on resid = down_proj column j * silu(gate_j) * delta_j. The silu(gate_j) factor varies per token; if gate_j is typically positive for that feature, it's ≈ multiplicative positive scaling — steering still roughly constant times positive scalar. Meh, less controlled.

Cleaner: do the mlp_act read (pass 3). We have 10 passes; using 3 for analysis is OK (leaves 5-6 for test iterations + buffer).

But wait: is constant steering toward d ("correct trace direction") even the best? Alternative use of same machinery: steer toward "answer direction": e.g., mean resid difference between positions where model is "computing/verifying" vs "rambling"? Too fancy.

Alternative intervention with potentially bigger, more reliable effect: per-head v_proj scaling? Nah.

Honestly, empirical iteration on alpha with paired eval is the core loop. Let me also consider a second intervention family to test if steering fails: MLP "feature upscaling" for arithmetic features: From mlp_act read on digit-producing positions vs other positions, find features with high selectivity for digit output; scale their down_proj columns by factor 1.2-1.5. This could sharpen arithmetic. This uses same read data (mlp_act) + token strings to find digit positions. Two interventions, one analysis.

Also consider "answer-checking" boost: features active when model writes "= " verification.

Alright, also consider a cheap but often effective trick: scale down the entropy by sharpening... can't touch output.

Let me also consider the "overthinking/looping" failure: with presence penalty 1.5, long thinking may spiral. If cut fraction is high at 8192, at eval 32768 they'd finish — so cuts here may overstate failures. Use metric on non-cut + also consider tokens.

Also important: choose eval subset stratified: GSM8K 64, MATH 64 (levels 1-5). Use same subset for all comparisons; seed fixed → paired.

Hmm, one more powerful idea: Because generate("both") runs both models, I can test TWO candidate edits per pass by... no, "both" = original vs edited only. One edited variant per pass. 5 test passes → test up to 5 variants sequentially; alpha tuning uses 2.

Actually wait, I could test two variants in ONE pass? "edited" uses all saved edits together. If I save edit A on layer 13 and edit B on layer 21, "edited" includes both. To isolate, I'd need separate passes. But I can use clear_edit between passes. To attribute, test A alone, then A+B. Standard.

Total pass budget: P1 baseline; P2 resid read; P3 mlp_act read; P4 test v1 (both); P5 test v2 (both); P6 test v3 (both); P7 maybe tune; P8 final confirm. Leaves 2 spare. OK.

Actually, maybe reduce reads: combine P2 and P3? read takes one kind. Two passes needed. Could skip P2 resid and go straight to mlp_act? The correctness direction better measured in resid (where steering lands). But actually for down_proj rank-1 steering, u lives in resid space (down output), v in mlp_act space. We need d in resid space (from P2) and v in mlp_act (from P3). Both needed. Alternatively use attn o_proj: u in resid, v in attn_out space — needs "attn_out" read. Choose MLP route (mlp_act read) since MLP outputs are simpler (no head structure) and DeltaNet linear-attn layers... o_proj input for DeltaNet is the delta-net state output; fine either way.

Hmm, wait. Actually there's an even simpler steering vector injection point: q/k/v/o of attention — no. What about adding steering through gate_proj? Same as up.
